lessons.title: N-400: Time outside the U.S.
context: Before your interview, make a list of every trip outside the United States: where you went, the day you left and the day you came back.
If you don't remember the dates, look at photos from your trips, the stamps in your passport, flight confirmation emails, bank or card statements, and frequent flyer accounts.
You can also see your recent trips on the I-94 website of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP): https://i94.cbp.dhs.gov. It is fast, but it may not show every trip.
If you still can't find the dates, you can ask CBP for your official travel record with a FOIA request. It takes a long time, so try the other ways first.

lessons.title: N-400: Immigration history
context: These questions use legal words for things many people know from life.
Detained: held by the police or immigration officers and not free to leave.
Removed or deported: forced by the U.S. government to leave the country.
Removal proceedings: a case before an immigration judge, where the government tries to make a person leave the country.
These questions ask about your whole life. If any of this ever happened to you, talk to a lawyer before you file.

lessons.title: N-400: Selective Service and the military
context: Everyone answers question 22.a on the form: “Are you a male who lived in the United States at any time between your 18th and 26th birthdays?”
Question 22.b is only for people who answered “Yes” to 22.a. So if you are not a man, 22.b doesn't apply to you.
The Selective Service is the U.S. list of men who could be called to serve in the military if the country needs them.
The questions after 22.b, about the U.S. armed forces, are for everyone.

lessons.title: N-400: Oath questions
context: Questions 35 to 37 start with “If the law requires it.” They do not ask you to join the military now. They ask if you would be willing, if a law ever required it.
These are the same promises you make in the Oath of Allegiance at your naturalization ceremony.
Bear arms: carry and use weapons for the United States, as a soldier.
Noncombatant service: work in the military that is not fighting, such as caring for wounded soldiers.
Work of national importance under civilian direction: important work for the country that is not military, led by people who are not in the military.
If a religious or moral reason means you could not make one of these promises, talk to a lawyer before you file.
